objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain how a pressurization system works and fails, teach the physiology of a decompression (impairment, hypoxia symptoms, time of useful consciousness and what a rapid decompression does to people), and plan and give the 14 CFR 61.31(g) ground and flight training, including a safe simulated rapid decompression.
why: The 61.31(g) training exists because the NTSB tied a series of fatal accidents to crews who lacked high-altitude knowledge and proficiency [[11:9|AC 61-107B 1-7]]. After a rapid decompression at 25,000 ft a pilot may have only 1.5 to 2.5 minutes of useful consciousness [[11:29|AC 61-107B Figure 2-3]], and pilots wrongly believe hypoxia is easy to spot [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. The instructor who signs the endorsement is the one who has to make the masks-first reflex stick.

key_terms.def: An aircraft whose service ceiling or maximum operating altitude, whichever is lower, is above 25,000 ft MSL [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]].

The altitude a pressurized aircraft must not operate above, set by flight, structural, powerplant, functional or equipment characteristics and listed in the AFM with the service ceiling [[11:10|AC 61-107B 2-1]].
Compressing air in the cabin to hold a cabin altitude lower than the actual flight altitude [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9]].
The largest difference between cabin and outside pressure that the pressurized section can support; each pressurized aircraft has its own [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9]].
Oxygen deficiency in the blood, tissues and cells great enough to impair body functions [[11:22|AC 61-107B 2-7]].
Something an observer can detect in a hypoxic person, such as rapid breathing or cyanosis [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]].
A sensation the hypoxic person can detect, such as air hunger, tingling or euphoria [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]].
A person's own order and intensity of hypoxia symptoms, which usually stays constant over the years [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

key_terms.term: Time of useful consciousness (TUC) or effective performance time (EPT)
key_terms.def: The time from losing the oxygen supply until a person can no longer take proper corrective and protective action [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7]].
A pressure loss that may go undetected; warning systems generally give the indication [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11]].
Breathing faster and deeper than needed, which upsets blood acid-base balance; its symptoms are easily confused with hypoxia [[11:22|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

The flight instruction form of demonstration-performance: instructor tells and does, learner tells while instructor does, then learner tells and does [[25:176|AIH 9-6]] [[25:177|AIH 9-7]] [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

chunks.title: What this Task asks of an instructor

body.p: As a CFI you will meet this Task mostly as the 61.31(g) checkout: a pilot moving into a pressurized airplane whose service ceiling or maximum operating altitude, whichever is lower, is above 25,000 ft MSL. That pilot may not act as PIC until an authorized instructor has given and logged ground training and flight training and signed an endorsement for each [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]].

The rule came out of a series of fatal accidents in which the NTSB believed a lack of high-altitude knowledge and proficiency led to loss of control. AC 61-107B chapter 2 is the FAA's recommended outline of training that meets 61.31(g) [[11:9|AC 61-107B 1-7]] [[11:10|AC 61-107B 2-1]].

head: ACS element
What the examiner wants to hear and see from you
rows: K1
How the system works and how it fails, explained so a learner can follow it (ACS AI.II.O.K1)
K2a to K2d
Impairment, hypoxia symptoms, TUC, and what a rapid decompression does to crew and passengers (ACS AI.II.O.K2)
R1, R2
The risks of high-altitude flight and of a pressurization malfunction, and how you manage them in training (ACS AI.II.O.R1, R2)
S1, S2
Operate the system and respond to simulated malfunctions while instructing; only if the airplane has the equipment (ACS AI.II.O.S1, S2)

callout.text: Most CFI checkride airplanes are not pressurized, so S1 and S2 drop out and R2 applies only if equipment is installed. Expect the examiner to have you teach this Task on the ground: bring a lesson plan built on the AC 61-107B outline [[11:11|AC 61-107B 2-2]].

The AC highly recommends the same training for every pilot who flies above 10,000 ft MSL, not only those 61.31(g) covers [[11:10|AC 61-107B 2-1]]. Offer it to any learner who flies high, pressurized or not.

check.q: What does AC 61-107B chapter 2 give an instructor?
check.a: An outline of recommended high-altitude ground and flight training that meets 61.31(g), from which the actual training can be built [[11:10|AC 61-107B 2-1]].

chunks.title: K1: Teaching how the system works

body.p: Start with one sentence the learner can repeat: pressurization compresses air in the cabin so the cabin altitude stays lower than the flight altitude [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9]]. Then add the parts. Air comes in from engine bleed air on turbine airplanes, and on most pressurized light airplanes from the turbocharger's compressor or an engine-driven pneumatic pump. An outflow valve lets air out and keeps the pressure constant by releasing the excess [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9]].

Build from what the learner already knows. When a skill relates to things already learned, the known-to-unknown strategy works well [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Most light piston airplanes that fly above 25,000 ft are turbocharged [[11:36|AC 61-107B 2-9]], so begin with the turbocharger the learner already understands and show where its air goes in the figure.

bullets: Cabin altitude: the cabin pressure stated as an equivalent altitude. Differential pressure: cabin pressure minus outside pressure [[1:195|PHAK 7-35]].
A typical system holds about an 8,000 ft cabin at the airplane's maximum designed cruising altitude [[1:195|PHAK 7-35]].

Isobaric range: the regulator holds the cabin pressure the pilot selected. Differential range: it limits cabin pressure to a preset differential, and once the structural maximum is reached, a further climb raises the cabin altitude too [[1:195|PHAK 7-35]] [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]].

The safety valve combines pressure relief, vacuum relief and the dump valve [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]. Some airplanes have a negative pressure relief valve that keeps cabin pressure from going below outside pressure after a sudden decompression or in a rapid descent [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9]].
The pilot must know the airplane's maximum differential and the manifold pressure settings recommended for various differentials [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9]].

callout.text: A pressurized airplane still needs supplemental oxygen, because decompression is always possible [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9]]. Learners who move up from unpressurized airplanes sometimes think the cabin replaces the masks. Say this early.
Have the learner draw the system from memory: one source in, one controlled exit, one safety valve, and the gauges. Errors in the drawing show you exactly what to reteach (application).

check.q: What does the outflow valve do in a pressurization system?
check.a: It regulates the flow of compressed air out of the cabin and keeps the pressure constant by releasing the excess to the atmosphere [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9]].

chunks.title: K1 and R2: Failure modes, and how a learner meets them

body.p: Decompression is the system's inability to hold its designed pressure differential. It comes from a malfunction of the system itself or from structural damage [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]] [[11:40|AC 61-107B 2-11]]. Teach the failure modes by what the learner will notice first.

head: Failure mode
What happens
First clue the learner gets
rows: Structural failure (window, door, fuselage)
Explosive or rapid decompression; air, dust and loose items rush toward the opening [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7]]
Small leak (for example a leaking door seal; application)
A slow decompression that may go undetected [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11]]
Often only the warning system or the cabin altimeter [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11]] [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]; a leaky door seal can also make noise [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7]]
Turbocharger failure when the cabin air depends on it
Possible loss of pressurization and a slow decompression during the descent [[11:42|AC 61-107B 2-11]]
Higher oil temperature, lower oil pressure, falling manifold pressure [[11:42|AC 61-107B 2-11]]
Climbing past the maximum differential
Not a failure, but the cabin altitude now climbs with the airplane [[1:195|PHAK 7-35]] [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]
Differential gauge at its limit; cabin altimeter rising (application)

bullets: Explosive decompression: cabin pressure changes faster than the lungs can decompress. Most authorities call anything under 0.5 seconds explosive. It is more likely in small-volume cabins and often results in lung damage [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11]].
Rapid decompression: the lungs decompress faster than the cabin, so the risk of lung damage is significantly lower than in an explosive one [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11]].
Gradual or slow decompression: dangerous because it may not be detected; automatic visual and aural warnings generally give the indication [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11]].

What sets the rate, all else equal: a larger opening, a smaller cabin and a higher altitude make it faster; a greater pressure differential makes it slower; and compressors that keep running slow the loss [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

body.p: Cabin size changes the clock. With the same hole, a typical small pressurized airplane can decompress on the order of 10 to 200 times faster than a large transport, so its crew will probably have less time for lifesaving actions [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11]]. A learner coming from airline flying needs to hear this: the same failure is more urgent in the small airplane.

Warnings: pressurized aircraft that meet certain Part 23 or Part 25 requirements have a cabin altitude warning that activates at a 10,000 ft cabin, and many airplanes have automatic visual and aural warnings of an unintentional pressure loss [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9]].

callout.text: Give the learner the airplane's AFM and have them find, aloud, what warns them, at what cabin altitude, and what the emergency checklist says to do first. This makes K1 specific to the airplane they will fly (application).

check.q: Why can a turbocharger failure lead to hypoxia in some pressurized piston airplanes?
check.a: If the pressurization depends on the turbocharger compressor, cabin pressure can be lost, and a slow decompression during the descent can bring on hypoxia unless the pilot monitors cabin pressure closely [[11:42|AC 61-107B 2-11]].

chunks.title: K2 and K2a: Impairment comes first, not last

body.p: Impairment is the heart of K2. The brain is one of the first organs hypoxia affects, and its higher reasoning parts degrade first, so judgment and thinking skills drop from the very start [[11:22|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. Teach this before symptoms: the faculty the learner would use to notice the problem is the first one to go.

bullets: From 12,000 to 15,000 ft cabin altitude, judgment, memory, alertness, coordination and the ability to calculate are impaired, and performance can seriously deteriorate within 15 minutes at 15,000 ft [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]].
Impairment is a continuum with no altitude where it clearly starts or stops, so if hypoxia is suspected, descend below 10,000 ft MSL [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]] [[11:26|AC 61-107B 2-7]].
Impairment grows with altitude, with harder and more complex tasks, and with new tasks compared with learned, practiced ones [[11:30|AC 61-107B 2-7]].
TUC does not mean the moment you pass out. Impaired performance may be immediate [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

body.p: Things that lower tolerance: carbon monoxide, anemia, some medicines, small amounts of alcohol, and depressant drugs; heat, cold, fever and anxiety raise oxygen demand [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]]. A smoker's physiological altitude at sea level is about 7,000 ft, so the AC says to set a lower cabin altitude when heavy smokers are aboard [[11:23|AC 61-107B 2-7]] [[11:24|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. The PHAK cites research that one ounce of alcohol can equate to about 2,000 ft of extra physiological altitude [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]; treat it as a rough rule, not a precise conversion.

callout.text: The teaching point: because new and complex tasks suffer most [[11:30|AC 61-107B 2-7]], the response to a decompression must already be a practiced habit. Practice builds automaticity, so less attention is needed to do the task [[25:75|AIH 3-24]]. The AC says mask donning should be practiced from time to time [[11:29|AC 61-107B Figure 2-3]].

check.q: Why is the faculty a learner would use to notice hypoxia the first one to suffer?
check.a: The brain is one of the first organs affected, and its higher reasoning parts degrade first, so judgment and thinking skills drop from the very start [[11:22|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

chunks.title: K2b: Symptoms of hypoxia and the personal signature

body.p: The AC splits the picture in two. Signs are what an observer can see; they are not much help for spotting hypoxia in yourself. Symptoms are what the hypoxic person feels [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. As an instructor you watch for signs in your learner; your learner must learn their own symptoms.

bullets: Euphoria, a false sense of well-being, is probably the most dangerous symptom [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]].
Visual impairment is probably the least reliable, because the visual field changes so slowly it can go unnoticed [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]].
Apart from possible headache and nausea, the symptoms are not uncomfortable, and the onset is usually insidious; being busy flying can let it go past the point of self-help [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]].
The PHAK adds decreased response, increased reaction time, drowsiness, numbness, narrowing vision and trouble reading instruments, with a false belief that everything is normal [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].

callout.text: The AC calls it a common, misleading and dangerous misconception that hypoxia is easy to recognize and fix before serious impairment [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. When a learner says 'I'd know', that is the misconception talking.

body.p: Symptoms differ between people, but a person's own order and intensity usually stay the same for years, which is the main benefit of chamber training [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]] [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]]. Altitude chamber training is not required but highly recommended [[11:17|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. The FAA CAMI one-day course demonstrates a rapid decompression from 8,000 to 18,000 ft and hypoxia at 25,000 ft in a chamber [[11:35|AC 61-107B 2-8]]; attendees must be at least 18, hold a current medical certificate and not have a cold [[11:36|AC 61-107B 2-8]].

Hyperventilation is easily confused with hypoxia and is an early response to it. Treat both at once: 100 percent oxygen under pressure, slow the rate and depth of breathing, check the oxygen equipment, and descend [[11:22|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. Breathing 100 percent oxygen will not worsen hyperventilation [[11:42|AC 61-107B 2-11]].

callout.text: Finger pulse oximeters help, but the FAA cautions against using them as the only indicator: waiting for the number to drop can mean waiting until impaired, and finger readings may not match oxygen reaching the brain [[11:26|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

check.q: Your learner is flushed, breathing fast and trembling, but says she feels great. What do the AC's terms call what you see and what she feels?
check.a: Rapid breathing and trembling are signs (an observer sees them); feeling great is euphoria, a symptom, and probably the most dangerous one [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

chunks.title: K2c: Time of useful consciousness as a planning tool

body.p: TUC, also called effective performance time, runs from the loss of oxygen until the person can no longer take proper corrective and protective action. The faster the ascent, the worse and faster the impairment, and TUC also falls as altitude rises [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. The PHAK describes it as the most time to make and carry out rational, life-saving decisions without supplemental oxygen [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].

bullets: After a decompression to between 25,000 and 43,000 ft, assume TUC is cut by 50 percent. Above 43,000 ft it is about 9 to 12 seconds, the time for blood to go from lung to brain plus the brain's reserve oxygen [[11:29|AC 61-107B Figure 2-3]].
The values are averages with wide individual variation, so the safest approach is to assume the lower value limits you [[11:29|AC 61-107B Figure 2-3]].

TUC also shrinks with physical activity, fatigue, low blood sugar, alcohol, medicines, smoking, poor condition and illness; ten deep knee bends at 25,000 ft without a mask can halve it [[11:30|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

The AC's emergency procedure for hypoxia: don the mask in 5 seconds or less, check for flow, breathe 100 percent oxygen; descend, preferably below 10,000 ft; land as soon as possible where medical help can be found [[11:27|AC 61-107B Table 2-6]].

body.p: Teach TUC as a planning number, not a trivia fact. Have the learner read the table for their planned cruise altitude, take the lower value after a rapid decompression, and then say what has to happen inside that time. The answer always starts with the mask, never with troubleshooting (application).

callout.text: Find your altitude, take the low number, and remember a rapid decompression costs at least half of it. The right-hand column of Figure 2-3 already shows that cut, so do not halve it again [[11:30|AC 61-107B 2-7]] [[11:29|AC 61-107B Figure 2-3]].

check.q: Why does the AC tell pilots to plan with the lower TUC value?
check.a: TUCs are averages with wide variation between people from factors the pilot will mostly not know, so the safest approach is to assume the lower value is limiting [[11:29|AC 61-107B Figure 2-3]].

chunks.title: K2d: Effects of rapid decompression on crew and passengers

body.p: Effects of rapid decompression on crew and passengers are what the learner will feel and see in the first seconds. Teach each one with what to do about it, so the surprise does not freeze them.

head: Effect
What happens
What you teach
rows: Lungs

Air escapes through the nose and mouth as outside pressure drops [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11]]; if the breath is held during a rapid altitude increase, lung gas expands with no way out and can damage the lungs [[11:21|AC 61-107B Table 2-2]]
Expect the rush of air; do not hold your breath (application from Table 2-2)
Ears
Pressure across the eardrum should clear automatically [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11]]
Ear pain in the later descent is an equalizing problem, not part of the decompression [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]]
Fog
Rapid drop in temperature and change in relative humidity [[11:40|AC 61-107B 2-11]]
Do not mistake fog for smoke; masks first (application)
Wind blast and cold
Felt as a wind blast; temperature drops as the air leaves [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7]]
Expect it; it is not a reason to delay the mask (application)
Debris
With a large opening, anything not secured moves toward it and can injure people [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7]]
Secure baggage and oxygen cylinders before flight [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11]]
Gas expansion
Most noticeable in the ears and the GI tract [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7]]
Discomfort is expected; do not let it distract from oxygen
Shorter TUC
Oxygen in the lungs is exhaled fast, reducing effective performance time [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]
Mask on in 5 seconds or less [[11:27|AC 61-107B Table 2-6]]
Decompression sickness
Rapid decompression above 18,000 ft raises the risk of altitude DCS [[11:33|AC 61-107B 2-7]]; it can happen in a pressurized airplane [[11:34|AC 61-107B 2-7]]
Do not fly for at least 24 hours after a real rapid decompression, and watch for delayed signs [[11:34|AC 61-107B 2-7]]
People near openings
Can be tossed or blown out after structural damage [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]
Anyone seated near an opening wears a seat belt or harness at all times while the airplane is pressurized [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]

body.p: For passengers: Part 25 airplanes meeting the stricter requirements drop masks automatically before a 15,000 ft cabin [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9]]. The AC names no such device for smaller airplanes, so in the airplanes your learners fly, the passengers may have to find and don their own masks (application). That makes the pilot's passenger briefing part of the decompression response.

callout.text: Breathing 100 percent oxygen in flight without prebreathing before takeoff does not prevent altitude DCS, and symptoms that go away in the descent may confirm DCS rather than rule it out [[11:35|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

check.q: After a real in-flight rapid decompression, how long does AC 61-107B say to wait before flying again?
check.a: At least 24 hours, staying alert for delayed signs of altitude DCS and seeking medical attention right away if they appear [[11:34|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

chunks.title: R1: The risks of high-altitude flight

body.p: The high-altitude environment starts below 25,000 ft. Flight levels begin at 18,000 ft, and above 10,000 ft a high-altitude pilot works in Class E up to FL 180 and Class A from FL 180 to FL 600 [[11:12|AC 61-107B 2-4]]. Teach the risks as a list the learner manages on every flight.

head: Risk
What the source says
How the learner manages it
rows: Clear air turbulence and wind shear
CAT gives no visual warning; a 40 kt horizontal change within 150 NM or vertical shear of 6 kt or more per 1,000 ft usually means moderate to severe turbulence [[11:14|AC 61-107B 2-5]]
Check PIREPs, one of the best sources of high-altitude turbulence and icing reports [[11:14|AC 61-107B 2-5]]
Thin-air handling
Controls feel sluggish near the absolute altitude, which is why most airplanes flying above 25,000 ft have an autopilot [[11:40|AC 61-107B 2-10]]
Know the airplane's handling and the autopilot
Automation in the climb
Vertical speed mode holds the rate and lets speed decay, which can lead toward a stall [[11:45|AC 61-107B 2-12]]
Watch airspeed and energy state in the climb [[11:45|AC 61-107B 2-12]]
Automation complacency
Pressurization systems can run without pilot adjustment [[30:50|RMH 7-1]], and automation can lull pilots into complacency [[30:51|RMH 7-2]]
Anticipate, act, verify [[30:51|RMH 7-2]]; monitor cabin pressure through climb and cruise [[11:45|AC 61-107B 2-12]]
Engine cooling
Hurried descents can overcool engines; light twins and pistons may need power to avoid cold shock [[11:15|AC 61-107B 2-6]]
Plan gradual descents early [[11:15|AC 61-107B 2-6]]
Weather below
Arrivals, departures and emergency diversions happen in low-altitude weather [[11:15|AC 61-107B 2-6]]
Check all charts, including low-level ones [[11:15|AC 61-107B 2-6]]
Oxygen for the descent

Above FL 250 at least a 10-minute supply for each occupant for a descent after losing pressure, beyond 91.211(a) [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]; stress raises breathing rate, so carry extra when possible [[11:14|AC 61-107B 2-6]] [[11:15|AC 61-107B 2-6]]
Plan oxygen, route and terrain together (application)

callout.text: Teach R1 with scenarios rather than lists. Scenario-based training aims to improve decision-making by challenging the learner with varied flight situations [[25:154|AIH 7-10]], and the instructor turns planning over to the learner as soon as possible, acting as a mentor once they start deciding [[25:155|AIH 7-11]].

check.q: Why should a learner pull PIREPs before a high-altitude flight?
check.a: CAT gives no visual warning, and PIREPs are one of the best ways to get timely, accurate icing and turbulence reports at high altitude [[11:14|AC 61-107B 2-5]].

chunks.title: R2: Malfunction risks, in flight and in training

body.p: A pressurization malfunction is a risk to manage twice: in the learner's future flights and in your own training flights.

bullets: Slow decompression is as dangerous as or more dangerous than a rapid one: the noise and fog may be missing, and hypoxia dulls the ability to see the emergency [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7]] [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7]].
Recovery from every type is similar and depends on recognizing it: the event, the cabin altitude warning, or hypoxia symptoms [[11:42|AC 61-107B 2-11]].
In the descent, reaching a safe altitude comes first, but a high-altitude rapid descent can cold-shock a piston engine and crack cylinders [[11:42|AC 61-107B 2-11]].
Fly the emergency descent within VNE, VLE and VFE, and VA in turbulence [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].
A learner with a cold risks an ear or sinus block, most often in the descent; prevention is not flying with an upper respiratory infection [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]].

head: Training risk
Control
rows: Actually depressurizing to 'make it real'
Never. The AC says an actual decompression is extremely dangerous and must never be done on purpose for training [[11:45|AC 61-107B 2-12]]
Leaving an assigned altitude in a practice descent
Coordinate with ATC before any practice emergency descent, and do not leave an assigned altitude without a clearance [[11:45|AC 61-107B 2-12]]
Engine damage from repeated descents
End the training descent once it is established and stable; prolonged practice overcools piston cylinders [[24:358|AFH 18-9]]
An anxious learner fighting the controls
Guard the controls and take them with 'I have the flight controls'; anxious learners can be very strong [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]
Fear of the maneuver
Stress safety and ease the learner into feared flight regions carefully [[25:39|AIH 2-6]]

callout.text: If the cabin warning sounds for real during a training flight, the simulation is over: both of you mask up and fly the real procedure. Agree on this in the preflight briefing (application).

check.q: What does the AC say about actually depressurizing the airplane for training?
check.a: Do not do it for this or any training; an actual decompression can be extremely dangerous and should never be done intentionally [[11:45|AC 61-107B 2-12]].

body.p: The rule lists the minimum ground subjects. Map each one to the AC outline so nothing is missed [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]] [[11:11|AC 61-107B 2-2]].

head: 61.31(g)(1) subject
Where to teach it from
rows: (i) High-altitude aerodynamics and meteorology
(ii) Respiration
(iii) Effects, symptoms and causes of hypoxia and any other high-altitude sickness
AC 61-107B 2-7d, hypoxia types, signs and treatment [[11:22|AC 61-107B 2-7]]; altitude DCS in 2-7e [[11:30|AC 61-107B 2-7]]
(iv) Duration of consciousness without supplemental oxygen
(v) Effects of prolonged usage of supplemental oxygen
Not in the AC outline; the AFH outline only names it [[24:308|AFH 15-14]]. No source in this course describes the effects, so bring current FAA aeromedical material
(vi) Causes and effects of gas expansion and gas bubble formation
(vii) Preventive measures for gas expansion, bubble formation and high-altitude sickness
Trapped gas treatment (Table 2-3) [[11:22|AC 61-107B Table 2-3]], hypoxia prevention [[11:26|AC 61-107B 2-7]] and DCS precautions [[11:34|AC 61-107B 2-7]]
(viii) Physical phenomena and incidents of decompression
(ix) Other physiological aspects
For example vision and glare at altitude [[11:35|AC 61-107B 2-7]]

body.p: The AC adds two things the rule does not spell out: the need to don masks immediately when the cabin altitude warning sounds, and the history and causes of past accidents, using NTSB reports [[11:12|AC 61-107B 2-3]]. Real accidents make the lesson vivid; immediate, dramatic learning tied to a real situation teaches more than routine material [[25:64|AIH 3-13]].

Make the physics concrete. Table 2-1 ties each gas law to the body: Boyle's law to trapped gas, Dalton's law to hypoxia, Henry's law to decompression sickness [[11:18|AC 61-107B Table 2-1]]. Henry's law is easy to show with a soft drink: open the cap and the dissolved gas comes out as bubbles [[11:30|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

callout.text: The ground training must be received and logged from an authorized instructor, who endorses that it was satisfactorily accomplished [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]]. 14 CFR 61.1 counts a ground instructor as an authorized instructor only when current under 61.217 and conducting ground training within the privileges and limitations of that certificate [[60:184|14 CFR 61.1]] [[12:30|AC 61-65K 37]]; a CFI qualifies when current under 61.197 and within the CFI certificate's privileges. The endorsement wording (sample A.74 [[12:54|AC 61-65K A.74]]) is taught in AI.II.K.

check.q: What two things does AC 61-107B 2-3 add to the ground training beyond the rule's subject list?
check.a: The need to don oxygen masks immediately when the cabin altitude warning activates, and the history and causes of past accidents and incidents [[11:12|AC 61-107B 2-3]].

chunks.title: S1: Operating the system, taught from the right seat

body.p: The flight training must be logged from an authorized instructor in a pressurized aircraft, or in a full flight simulator or flight training device representative of one, and must include normal cruise above 25,000 ft MSL [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]]. If an airplane is used, each flight should have a preflight briefing, flight planning, a preflight inspection, instructor demonstrations where needed, and a postflight discussion [[11:44|AC 61-107B 2-12]].

head: Phase
What the learner does
What you emphasize
rows: Preflight
Inspect fuselage, windshield and windows for cracks; set up and test the oxygen, including talking to ATC through the mask [[11:44|AC 61-107B 2-12]]
Damage that could rupture under pressurization [[11:44|AC 61-107B 2-12]]
Takeoff and climb
Follow the AFM power settings and airspeeds; set pressurization as the manufacturer recommends [[11:44|AC 61-107B 2-12]] [[11:14|AC 61-107B 2-6]]
Avoid overboost [[11:44|AC 61-107B 2-12]]
Climb above 25,000 ft
Fly the transition repeatedly; adjust pressurization with altitude; set 29.92 at FL 180 [[11:45|AC 61-107B 2-12]]
Energy state and automation management [[11:45|AC 61-107B 2-12]]
Cruise
Monitor cabin pressurization the whole time [[11:45|AC 61-107B 2-12]]; keep the differential below its maximum [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]
Cabin altitude, cabin rate and differential, not just the airplane altimeter
Planned descent
Gradual, with cabin rate generally no more than 500 or 600 fpm and the cabin equal to outside pressure before landing [[11:15|AC 61-107B 2-6]]
Equalizing cabin and outside pressure [[11:45|AC 61-107B 2-12]]
Shutdown
Cool the turbocharged engine at least 1 minute; turn off oxygen valves [[11:45|AC 61-107B 2-12]]
Leaving the system ready for the next pilot

body.p: Use telling-and-doing. On the first flight you explain and demonstrate each controller setting in the order you described it. Next the learner tells you what to set while you do it, which lets you catch misunderstandings before they are flying; then the learner tells and does [[25:177|AIH 9-7]] [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

callout.text: During 'learner tells, instructor does', ask the learner to predict the gauge readings before you move the controller. A wrong prediction shows a misconception you can fix on the spot, which matters because what is learned first is hard to undo [[25:178|AIH 9-8]] [[25:64|AIH 3-13]].

check.q: What does the AC say each training flight in an airplane should include?
check.a: A preflight briefing, flight planning, a preflight inspection, instructor demonstrations of maneuvers or procedures when necessary, and a postflight briefing and discussion [[11:44|AC 61-107B 2-12]].

chunks.title: S2: Teaching the simulated rapid decompression

body.p: 61.31(g)(2) requires emergency procedures for a simulated rapid decompression, done without actually depressurizing, and emergency descent procedures [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]]. The AC calls for at least one of each [[11:45|AC 61-107B 2-12]], and the AFH outline stresses the immediate donning of masks [[24:309|AFH 15-15]].

bullets: On the ground: brief the AFM emergency procedure and the AC's procedure: mask in 5 seconds or less, check flow, 100 percent oxygen, descend, land as soon as possible where medical help is available [[11:27|AC 61-107B Table 2-6]].
Before the exercise: coordinate with ATC in advance; never leave an assigned altitude without a clearance [[11:45|AC 61-107B 2-12]].
Start the simulation: masks on, oxygen controls on, configure for the emergency descent, and start the descent as soon as possible [[11:45|AC 61-107B 2-12]].

Descent technique: make simulated descents in a turn to check for traffic below and look for a landing area, with about 30 to 45 degrees of bank to keep positive load factors, power to idle unless the manufacturer says otherwise, propeller to low pitch, gear and flaps as recommended [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].
In training, end the descent once it is established and stable [[24:358|AFH 18-9]], and start any recovery high enough for a safe level-off [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].
Afterward: postflight discussion, questions answered, next flight previewed [[11:45|AC 61-107B 2-12]].

body.p: Watch the effects of rapid decompression you taught in K2d as if they were real: the learner should breathe normally rather than hold a breath [[11:21|AC 61-107B Table 2-2]], ignore the simulated noise, and go for the mask before anything else. If the learner reaches for the controller or checklist first, stop and repeat it right then; a wrong first habit is very hard to unlearn [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

callout.text: Never depressurize the airplane to make the exercise realistic [[11:45|AC 61-107B 2-12]]. If a learner wants to feel a real decompression, send them to the chamber course, which demonstrates one safely [[11:35|AC 61-107B 2-8]].

check.q: How does the AC tell you to simulate a rapid decompression?
check.a: Don the oxygen masks, turn on the oxygen controls, configure for an emergency descent and fly it as soon as possible, after coordinating with ATC, without actually depressurizing [[11:45|AC 61-107B 2-12]].

chunks.title: How to teach it: lesson flow and sign-off

body.p: Deliver the flight portion with demonstration-performance: explanation, demonstration, learner performance with your supervision, and evaluation. Let the learner perform as soon as possible after your demonstration [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].

head: Lesson
Content
Ends with
rows: Ground 1
Environment, weather, flight planning and navigation [[11:11|AC 61-107B 2-2]]
Learner plans a high-altitude flight
Ground 2
Physiology: respiration, hypoxia, TUC, trapped gas, DCS, decompression; chamber optional [[11:11|AC 61-107B 2-2]]
Learner explains a decompression response from memory
Ground 3
Systems, the AFM, and emergencies [[11:11|AC 61-107B 2-2]]
Ground training endorsement when satisfactory [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]]
Flights
As many as needed to cover the AC flight items [[11:43|AC 61-107B 2-12]] [[11:44|AC 61-107B 2-12]]
Flight endorsement when proficient [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]]

body.p: Evaluate with collaborative assessment: the learner assesses first, then you compare it with your own detailed assessment. Point out what needs work with concrete suggestions, and try not to end on a negative note [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].

callout.text: Sign nothing until you have seen it. The rule needs a logged ground training endorsement certifying satisfactory completion and a logged flight training endorsement certifying the pilot is proficient [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]]. Exceptions for documented earlier experience are in 61.31(g)(3) [[60:215|14 CFR 61.31(g)(3)]].

check.q: In demonstration-performance, when should the learner first perform the skill?
check.a: As soon as possible after the demonstration [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Troubleshooting before oxygen
Hands go to the controller or checklist at the call
Stop and redo: mask in 5 seconds or less first [[11:27|AC 61-107B Table 2-6]]; drill until automatic [[25:75|AIH 3-24]]
'I'd know if I were hypoxic'
Learner shrugs off the physiology or the chamber
Show the AC warning about that misconception [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]] and recommend the chamber [[11:17|AC 61-107B 2-7]]
Fast breathing on the mask
Rapid, deep breaths after donning
Slow the rate and depth; 100 percent oxygen will not worsen hyperventilation [[11:42|AC 61-107B 2-11]]
Pulling the mask off when feeling worse
Learner says the oxygen 'isn't working'
After severe hypoxia, symptoms can seem worse for 15 to 60 seconds; keep breathing 100 percent slowly [[11:42|AC 61-107B 2-11]]
Starting a practice descent without clearance
Descent begins before ATC approves
Coordinate in advance; no leaving an assigned altitude without clearance [[11:45|AC 61-107B 2-12]]
Climbing in VS mode at high altitude
Airspeed bleeding off in the climb
Watch energy state; VS mode can lead to speed loss and stall [[11:45|AC 61-107B 2-12]]
Diving the cabin in normal descents
Cabin rate well above 500 to 600 fpm; ears hurting
Plan descents early; equalize before landing [[11:15|AC 61-107B 2-6]]
Overspeed in the emergency descent
Airspeed at VLE or VFE with gear or flaps out
Configure as the manufacturer says and respect VNE, VLE, VFE and VA [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]
Ignoring a quiet pressure loss
Cabin altimeter creeping up, no bang
Trust the warning and gauges; slow decompressions may not be noticed [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11]]

callout.text: Correct errors in a positive, timely way during practice, and do not hesitate to take control when needed; this is a learning phase, not an evaluation [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

check.q: After a severe hypoxia exposure your learner dons the mask and feels worse for about 30 seconds. What do you tell them?
check.a: This apparent worsening can last 15 to 60 seconds; keep breathing 100 percent oxygen slowly [[11:42|AC 61-107B 2-11]].

scenario.title: The owner who wants a quick sign-off
scenario.setup: A 600-hour commercial pilot bought a pressurized turbocharged piston single. Its AFM lists a maximum operating altitude of FL 250 and a service ceiling of FL 270, and he plans to buy a turboprop single with a maximum operating altitude of FL 300 next year. He has never flown a pressurized airplane. He asks you to train him for both, in as few flights as possible, and mentions he has a head cold this week.

questions.q: Does 61.31(g) apply to the piston single? To the turboprop?
questions.a: Not to the piston single: the lower of its two numbers is FL 250, and the rule needs that lower number to be above 25,000 ft MSL. It does apply to the turboprop, whose lower number is FL 300 [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]]. The AC still highly recommends the training for anyone flying above 10,000 ft MSL [[11:10|AC 61-107B 2-1]].

questions.q: What will your ground training cover?
questions.a: At least the 61.31(g)(1) subjects: high-altitude aerodynamics and meteorology, respiration, hypoxia, duration of consciousness without oxygen, prolonged oxygen use, gas expansion and bubbles, prevention, decompression, and other physiology [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]], built on the AC outline plus past accident histories and the need to don masks immediately at the cabin warning [[11:11|AC 61-107B 2-2]] [[11:12|AC 61-107B 2-3]].

questions.q: He says he would recognize hypoxia right away. How do you answer?
questions.a: The AC calls that a common, misleading and dangerous misconception; hypoxia is insidious and euphoria is the most dangerous symptom [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. Recommend a chamber course to learn his own hypoxia signature [[11:17|AC 61-107B 2-7]] [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

questions.q: Should you fly the training this week?
questions.a: No. A cold can cause an ear or sinus block, most often in the descent [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]], and the CAMI chamber course will not take someone with a cold either [[11:36|AC 61-107B 2-8]]. Reschedule (application).

questions.q: How many flights will the flight training take?
questions.a: As many as needed to cover the procedures, each with a preflight briefing, planning, inspection, any demonstrations and a postflight discussion [[11:43|AC 61-107B 2-12]] [[11:44|AC 61-107B 2-12]]. It must include cruise above 25,000 ft, a simulated rapid decompression without depressurizing, and an emergency descent [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]].

questions.q: In the simulated decompression he grabs the controller before his mask. What now?
questions.a: Stop and have him do it again with the mask first, in 5 seconds or less [[11:27|AC 61-107B Table 2-6]]. Fix it immediately, because the first way a procedure is learned is hard to change [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Sign the flight endorsement only when he is proficient [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]].

skills.do: If the airplane has a pressurization system, operate it from the right seat while explaining it as you would to a learner: set the controller per the AFM, and call out cabin altitude, cabin rate and differential, and what each tells you. The ACS gives no numeric tolerance for this element (ACS AI.II.O.S1).
skills.practice: Talk through a whole flight profile (preflight, climb, cruise above 25,000 ft, descent and equalization) using AC 61-107B 2-12 [[11:44|AC 61-107B 2-12]] [[11:45|AC 61-107B 2-12]], then do it again as 'learner tells, instructor does' with a fellow instructor playing the learner [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

skills.do: If installed, respond to a simulated pressurization malfunction while instructing: masks on and oxygen flowing first, then the AFM emergency descent within VNE, VLE, VFE and VA, with ATC coordinated, and explain each step. The ACS gives no numeric tolerance for this element (ACS AI.II.O.S2).
skills.practice: Time yourself donning the mask until it is under 5 seconds [[11:27|AC 61-107B Table 2-6]], and rehearse the coordinated, simulated descent sequence aloud [[11:45|AC 61-107B 2-12]] [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

quiz.q: A typical pressurization system holds about what cabin pressure altitude at the airplane's maximum designed cruising altitude?
quiz.why: A cabin pressurization system typically maintains a cabin pressure altitude of about 8,000 ft at the maximum designed cruising altitude, which prevents rapid changes of cabin altitude that may be uncomfortable or cause injury [[1:195|PHAK 7-35]].

quiz.q: With all other factors equal, what does a greater cabin pressure differential do to the rate of a decompression, per AC 61-107B?
options: Makes it faster
Makes it slower
Has no effect
Makes it explosive
quiz.why: The AC lists greater pressure differential as meaning slower decompression; a larger opening, a smaller cabin and higher altitude make it faster [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

quiz.q: Most authorities consider a decompression explosive when it happens in less than about how long?
options: 0.5 seconds
5 seconds
30 seconds
2 minutes
quiz.why: Any decompression in less than 0.5 seconds is considered explosive and potentially dangerous [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11]] [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]].

quiz.q: Some pressurized airplanes have a negative pressure relief valve. What does it do?
options: Opens to dump cabin air whenever the structural differential limit is reached, protecting the fuselage
Holds the cabin altitude the pilot selected while in the isobaric range
Stops cabin pressure from dropping below outside pressure in a decompression or rapid descent
Lets excess compressed air out to keep cabin pressure constant in cruise
quiz.why: Some aircraft have a negative pressure relief valve to equalize pressure in a sudden decompression or rapid descent, so the cabin pressure cannot become lower than the ambient pressure [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9]]. Limiting the differential is the pressure relief part of the safety valve [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]], and releasing excess air to hold the pressure is the outflow valve's job [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9]].

quiz.q: Which gas law does AC 61-107B use to explain decompression sickness?
options: Boyle's law
Dalton's law
Henry's law
Charles' law
quiz.why: Henry's law explains why nitrogen comes out of solution and forms bubbles as pressure drops; Boyle's explains trapped gas and Dalton's explains hypoxia [[11:18|AC 61-107B Table 2-1]].

quiz.q: Planning a flight in the flight levels, your learner studies the winds aloft. Which change does AC 61-107B say usually indicates moderate to severe turbulence?
options: Any wind over 100 kt at the planned altitude, whatever the direction
40 kt of horizontal change within 150 NM, or vertical shear of 6 kt or more per 1,000 ft
20 kt of horizontal change within 500 NM, or a temperature change of 2 C or more per 1,000 ft
A wind shift of more than 30 degrees between two reporting stations on the route
quiz.why: Horizontal wind changes of 40 kt within 150 NM or vertical wind shear of 6 kt or greater per 1,000 ft usually indicate moderate to severe turbulence and should be avoided [[11:14|AC 61-107B 2-5]].

quiz.q: How many simulated rapid decompressions does AC 61-107B say the flight training should include?
options: None; it is ground training only
At least one, along with an emergency descent
Exactly three
One, but only in a chamber
quiz.why: Training should include at least one simulated rapid decompression and emergency descent [[11:45|AC 61-107B 2-12]].

quiz.q: Why does AC 61-107B say most airplanes that fly above 25,000 ft MSL have an autopilot?
options: Because 61.31(g) requires one for any airplane with a pressurized cabin
Near the absolute altitude the controls feel sluggish, so altitude and heading are hard to hold
Because 91.211 bars hand-flying above FL 250 unless a second pilot is at the controls and masked
Because the thin air makes the controls too sensitive to move by hand
quiz.why: The reduced weight of air moving over the control surfaces at high altitude decreases their effectiveness. As the airplane approaches its absolute altitude the controls feel sluggish, making altitude and heading difficult to maintain, so most airplanes that fly above 25,000 ft MSL are equipped with an autopilot [[11:40|AC 61-107B 2-10]].

quiz.q: Under the 14 CFR 61.1 definition, when is a certificated ground instructor an 'authorized instructor'?
options: Always, for any training under part 61
When current under 61.217 and giving ground training within the privileges and limitations of the ground instructor certificate
Only when a CFI countersigns the logbook
Never; only flight instructors are authorized instructors
quiz.why: That is paragraph (i) of the definition [[60:184|14 CFR 61.1]], repeated in AC 61-65K [[12:30|AC 61-65K 37]].

quiz.q: Your learner had joint pain at altitude that went away in the descent. What does AC 61-107B say about that?
options: It rules out DCS
It may actually confirm altitude DCS; get a medical evaluation
It means the cabin was set too low
It is normal trapped gas in the joints and needs no follow-up after landing
quiz.why: Do not ignore signs that go away in the descent; that could confirm altitude DCS, and any case should be medically evaluated [[11:35|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

final_quiz.q: A pilot's only pressurized experience is PIC time logged in 1995 in a pressurized single with a maximum operating altitude of FL 300. He wants to fly a similar airplane now. What about 61.31(g)?
options: Exempt, because he has pressurized PIC time
Exempt, because the time was over 20 years ago
He needs the training and endorsements; the PIC-time exception covers only time before April 15, 1991
He needs only the ground training
final_quiz.why: The (g)(3) exceptions cover PIC service or a proficiency check before April 15, 1991, a military PIC check, or a Part 121, 125 or 135 PIC check [[60:215|14 CFR 61.31(g)(3)]]. 1995 PIC time fits none of them, so (g)(1) and (g)(2) apply [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]].

final_quiz.q: At FL 260 on your training flight, Center has you at an assigned altitude. You call 'simulated decompression' and the learner dons the mask and immediately pushes over. You did not brief ATC. What is the right instructor action?
options: Let it continue; the training is worth it
Stop the descent and hold the altitude; coordinate with ATC before any practice descent
Declare an emergency so the practice descent becomes legal, then cancel it at the bottom
Switch to 121.5 and continue
final_quiz.why: Coordinate with ATC in advance of any practice emergency descent and do not vacate an assigned altitude without a clearance [[11:45|AC 61-107B 2-12]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner hurries the walk-around of the pressurized single. Which items does AC 61-107B say deserve particular attention on a high-altitude flight?
options: Tires and brakes
Fuselage, windshields, windows and canopies, for cracks that could rupture under pressure
Fuel caps and vents only
Antennas and static wicks, since static discharge rises with altitude and can damage avionics
final_quiz.why: The preflight inspection should give particular attention to the fuselage, windshields, window panels and canopies for cracks or damage that could rupture under the stress of pressurization [[11:44|AC 61-107B 2-12]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner flies a real emergency descent from FL 250 in a turbocharged piston single and worries about the engine. What does AC 61-107B say?
options: Engine damage is impossible in a descent, since the engine is at idle
Hold altitude until the cylinders cool slowly, then descend at 500 fpm to protect the engine first
A safe altitude comes first, though a rapid descent can cold-shock the engine and crack cylinders
Shut the engine down to protect it and glide to a lower altitude
final_quiz.why: Top priority is reaching a safe altitude, but pilots should be aware that cold shock in piston engines can result from a high-altitude rapid descent, causing cracked cylinders or other engine damage [[11:42|AC 61-107B 2-11a]].

final_quiz.q: Above 43,000 ft, what sets the roughly 9 to 12 seconds of useful consciousness after a rapid decompression?
options: The size of the hole
Blood circulation time from lungs to brain, plus the brain's reserve oxygen
How fast the outflow valve closes
Whether the pilot is a smoker, since smoking alone sets TUC above that altitude
final_quiz.why: Above 43,000 ft TUC drops to the lung-to-brain circulation time plus reserve oxygen stored in the brain, about 9 to 12 seconds [[11:29|AC 61-107B Figure 2-3]].

final_quiz.q: Before the first flight in his pressurized single, what does AC 61-107B say the pilot must know about pressure differentials?
options: Only the setting of the cabin altitude warning, since the controller manages every differential
The differential the cabin held on its last flight, from the maintenance log
Its maximum differential and the recommended manifold pressures for various differentials
Nothing beyond the POH checklist, since differential limits are for mechanics
final_quiz.why: Each pressurized aircraft has a determined maximum pressure differential that its pressurized section can support, and the pilot must be familiar with these limitations as well as the manifold pressure settings recommended for various pressure differentials [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9]].

final_quiz.q: After landing the turbocharged pressurized single, your learner pulls the mixture as soon as the airplane stops. What does AC 61-107B's shutdown item say?
options: Shut down at once to save fuel; turbochargers need no cooling time
Let the turbocharged engine cool for at least 1 minute, and turn off the oxygen valves
Run the engine at full power for 1 minute to clear the turbocharger first
Cool the engine for at least 10 minutes and leave the oxygen on so the next pilot is ready
final_quiz.why: Allow the turbocharged engine to cool for at least 1 minute and follow the AFM shutdown procedures. Before exiting, check that all oxygen equipment and valves are off or in the position the manufacturer recommends [[11:45|AC 61-107B 2-12]].

final_quiz.q: In a high-altitude climb using vertical speed mode, your learner's airspeed is steadily dropping. What is the risk you are teaching?
options: Overspeed
VS mode holds the climb rate while speed decays, which can lead toward a stall
Excessive cabin differential
Turbocharger overboost, because VS mode adds power automatically to hold the rate
final_quiz.why: VS mode prioritizes the commanded rate; speed decays when thrust available is less than required, with potential for stall [[11:45|AC 61-107B 2-12]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner finished the ground training and you endorsed it. Can she act as PIC of the pressurized airplane now?
options: Yes, the ground endorsement is enough for PIC; flight training is only recommended
Yes, if a CFI is on board
No; she also needs logged flight training and a proficiency endorsement
Yes, below FL 250 only
final_quiz.why: 61.31(g) requires both the ground training endorsement and the flight training endorsement [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner can schedule a full flight simulator that represents his pressurized airplane. Can the 61.31(g) flight training be done in it?
options: No, only in the airplane, because the training must include normal cruise above 25,000 ft
Yes; a full flight simulator or FTD representing a pressurized aircraft is allowed
Only the emergency descent
Only if a DPE is present
final_quiz.why: The flight training may be received in a pressurized aircraft or in a full flight simulator or flight training device representative of one [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner, moving from a turboprop to a pressurized piston single, asks where its cabin air comes from. What does AC 61-107B say?
options: Engine bleed air, the same source every pressurized airplane uses
On most pressurized light airplanes, the turbocharger's compressor or an engine-driven pneumatic pump
A separate electric compressor in the tail, so cabin pressure never depends on the engine or its turbocharger
Ram air through the outflow valve, which the controller opens to raise cabin pressure
final_quiz.why: Turbine aircraft use engine bleed air for pressurization; in most pressurized light aircraft the air comes from the turbocharger's compressor or an engine-driven pneumatic pump, and an outflow valve releases the excess to keep the pressure constant [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9]]. That is why a turbocharger failure can cost cabin pressure in some piston airplanes [[11:42|AC 61-107B 2-11a]].

final_quiz.q: Your new owner says that since the airplane is pressurized, he will leave the oxygen system out of his preflight. What does AC 61-107B say?
options: Correct; pressurized airplanes need no oxygen, since the cabin altitude warning gives time to descend
A pressurized airplane still needs oxygen, because decompression is always possible
Oxygen is needed only above FL 410
Only passengers need oxygen
final_quiz.why: Because of the ever-present possibility of decompression, a pressurized aircraft still requires supplemental oxygen [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9]]; the preflight should also check the oxygen equipment and supply [[11:44|AC 61-107B 2-12]].

final_quiz.q: At FL 240 your learner is chatty and cheerful. There has been no horn, but the cabin altimeter has crept from 8,000 to 13,000 ft over several minutes. What is happening, and what do you do?
options: A gauge error; ignore it until a horn sounds
A likely slow decompression with euphoria in the learner; masks on for both of you and descend
Normal cabin climb at maximum differential; continue
Hyperventilation; tell the learner to stop talking
final_quiz.why: A slow decompression may go undetected and is as dangerous as a rapid one [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11]] [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7]]; euphoria is probably the most dangerous hypoxia symptom [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. If hypoxia is suspected, don the mask, breathe 100 percent oxygen and descend [[11:26|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

takeaways: 61.31(g) applies when the lower of service ceiling and maximum operating altitude is above 25,000 ft MSL.
It needs logged ground training with an endorsement and logged flight training with a proficiency endorsement; wording is in AI.II.K.
Hypoxia hits judgment first, and the belief that it is easy to recognize is itself the danger.
Teach TUC as a planning number: lower value, halved after a rapid decompression.
Teach each effect of rapid decompression with what to do about it, so it does not startle the learner.
Simulate, never depressurize: masks, oxygen on, configure, descend, with ATC coordinated first.
Use telling-and-doing and fix a wrong first habit (troubleshooting before the mask) on the spot.
cfi_notes: 61.31(g)(1) and (2) each call for an endorsement (ground training satisfactorily accomplished, then flight proficiency) [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]], while the AC 61-65K sample A.74 is one statement that the pilot received 'the required training of 14 CFR 61.31(g)' and is proficient [[12:54|AC 61-65K A.74]], and AC 61-107B 2-1 also describes one endorsement after both trainings [[11:10|AC 61-107B 2-1]]. The sources do not say whether one combined entry or two entries is preferred. If the ground and flight training are given at different times or by different instructors, separate entries are the clear way to show both (application). Wording belongs to AI.II.K.

AC 61-107B 2-12 says the flight training may be done in a simulator meeting 121.407 or a high-altitude airplane [[11:43|AC 61-107B 2-12]]. The current rule says a pressurized aircraft or a full flight simulator or flight training device representative of one [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]]. Teach the rule.

The PHAK says rapid decompression cuts effective performance time 'by one-third to one-fourth its normal time' [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]; AC 61-107B says TUC falls by 50 percent from 25,000 to 43,000 ft and by at least 50 percent in a rapid decompression [[11:29|AC 61-107B Figure 2-3]] [[11:30|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. Teach the AC and Figure 2-3.

The PHAK says all pressurized aircraft have automatic visual and aural warnings [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]; the AC says many airplanes do, and only aircraft meeting certain Part 23 or 25 requirements have the 10,000 ft cabin warning [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9]]. Teach the AC and the learner's AFM.

TUC tables differ: the PHAK gives 30 minutes or more at 20,000 ft and 5 to 10 minutes at 22,000 ft [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]], the AIM says corrective action is lost in 5 to 12 minutes at 20,000 ft [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]], and the AC gives 10 minutes at 22,000 ft [[11:29|AC 61-107B Figure 2-3]]. Have learners plan with the AC figure and its lower values.

AC 61-107B is from 2013 (Change 1 in 2015) and names phone numbers, web addresses and services such as DUATS [[11:36|AC 61-107B 2-8]] [[11:44|AC 61-107B 2-12]] that may have changed. Check current FAA pages before sending a learner to the chamber course.

61.31(g)(1)(v) requires 'effects of prolonged usage of supplemental oxygen' [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]], but the AC 61-107B outline does not list it and the AFH outline only names it [[24:308|AFH 15-14]]. None of the sources in this course describe those effects, and the Supplemental Oxygen Task does not cover them either. Bring current FAA aeromedical material so the ground endorsement is complete.

On a CFI checkride in an unpressurized airplane, expect to teach this Task as a ground lesson. A one-page lesson plan that maps the 61.31(g) subjects to the AC paragraphs shows the examiner you can actually give the training.

The 61.1 definition counts a ground instructor as an authorized instructor only within the privileges of the ground instructor certificate [[60:184|14 CFR 61.1]], and 61.215 lists those privileges as knowledge-area training for certificates and ratings, flight review ground training and knowledge test recommendations, with no mention of 61.31(g) [[60:354|14 CFR 61.215]]. AC 61-107B speaks of the flight instructor who gave the training endorsing it [[11:10|AC 61-107B 2-1]]. Plan on a CFI giving and endorsing the 61.31(g) ground training; check with the FSDO before relying on a ground instructor.
gaps: No source gives a minimum number of hours or flights for 61.31(g) training; the AC says as many flights as necessary [[11:43|AC 61-107B 2-12]].

The sources do not say whether the instructor giving 61.31(g) flight training must have 61.31(g) training; if the instructor will act as PIC, the rule applies to the PIC (application). Check with the FSDO if in doubt.
Controller settings, maximum differential, warning thresholds and emergency descent configuration and speeds are airplane-specific; use the AFM/POH.
No source gives a standard instructor-to-learner callout for starting and ending a simulated decompression; agree on one in the preflight briefing.
The ACS sets no numeric tolerance for S1 or S2, and no source defines 'proficient' for the flight endorsement; that judgment is the instructor's.
No source in this course describes the 'effects of prolonged usage of supplemental oxygen' that 61.31(g)(1)(v) requires; get current FAA aeromedical material.

activities.title: Work the numbers you will teach
activities.intro: Work each one out, then type your answer.

items.q: At 28,000 ft the standard outside pressure is 4.8 psi. The cabin is held at 10.9 psi, an 8,000 ft cabin. What is the cabin differential pressure?
items.why: 10.9 - 4.8 = 6.1 psi differential, the PHAK's worked example [[1:195|PHAK 7-35]].

items.q: TUC at 30,000 ft is 1 to 2 minutes. Using the lower value and the AC's 50 percent rule for a rapid decompression, how many seconds do you plan on?
items.why: 1 min x 60 = 60 s; 60 x 0.5 = 30 s, the lower value shown following rapid decompression at 30,000 ft [[11:29|AC 61-107B Figure 2-3]] [[11:30|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

items.q: Cabin altitude is 7,500 ft and the destination field is at 1,500 ft. At a cabin descent rate of 600 fpm, how many minutes does the cabin need to equalize?
items.why: 7,500 - 1,500 = 6,000 ft; 6,000 / 600 = 10 minutes. Cabin rates should generally not exceed 500 or 600 fpm, and the cabin should equal outside pressure before landing [[11:15|AC 61-107B 2-6]].

items.q: From Table 2-8, a B-727 cabin is 9,045 cubic ft and an NA-265 cabin is 430 cubic ft. How many times bigger is the B-727 cabin? (Round to a whole number.)

The PHAK cites research that one ounce of alcohol can equate to about 2,000 ft of extra physiological altitude. A passenger had two ounces; the cabin is at 8,000 ft. Using that rough rule, about what physiological altitude is the passenger at?
items.why: 8,000 + 2 x 2,000 = 12,000 ft [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]. This is a rough teaching illustration, not a precise conversion.

activities.title: True or false: what a rapid decompression does
activities.intro: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

cards.s: In a decompression, the pressure across the eardrum should clear automatically.
Holding your breath during a rapid increase in altitude protects the lungs.
cards.why: False. The trapped lung gas expands with no way out and could cause lung damage [[11:21|AC 61-107B Table 2-2]].

cards.s: Breathing 100 percent oxygen during the flight, with no prebreathing before takeoff, prevents altitude DCS.
Altitude DCS can follow a rapid decompression in a pressurized airplane.
Cabin fog after a rapid decompression comes from the drop in temperature and change in humidity.
A slow decompression usually announces itself with noise and fog.
cards.why: False. Those phenomena may not be evident in a slow decompression [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

activities.title: Run the simulated rapid decompression
activities.intro: Put the training sequence in order, then tap Check.
steps: On the ground: brief the AFM procedure and how you will start the simulation
Coordinate the practice emergency descent with ATC
At altitude: call the simulated decompression (the cabin stays pressurized)
Learner dons the mask in 5 seconds or less and checks for flow
Oxygen controls on and the airplane configured for the descent
Fly the cleared descent within VNE, VLE, VFE and VA
End the descent once established and stable
Postflight: learner self-assessment, then your assessment

activities.title: Giving the flight training, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are giving 61.31(g) flight training in a pressurized turbocharged piston single, cruising at an assigned FL 260 with a learner who finished the ground training last week.

steps.s: Before the exercise, the learner says: 'Let's pull the dump valve for a second so I know what it feels like.'
options: Do it briefly at FL 260
Do it after descending to FL 200
Decline, and simulate it as the AC describes; suggest the chamber course
Do it with masks already on
steps.why: Actual decompression must never be done for training [[11:45|AC 61-107B 2-12]]; the chamber course demonstrates one safely [[11:35|AC 61-107B 2-8]].

steps.s: Center has approved your practice descent. You call 'simulated decompression' and the learner reaches for the pressurization controller.
options: Let them finish troubleshooting, then debrief
Call 'masks' and have them start over with the mask first
Take the controls and fly the rest yourself
Ignore it; it was only simulated
steps.why: The mask goes on first, in 5 seconds or less [[11:27|AC 61-107B Table 2-6]]. Correct a wrong first habit right away [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

steps.s: Mask on, oxygen flowing. The learner rolls into 60 degrees of bank with gear down and the airspeed near VLE.
options: Let it ride; faster is better
Coach about 30 to 45 degrees of bank and keep the airspeed below VLE
Retract the gear to go faster
Level the wings and stop the descent
steps.why: Use about 30 to 45 degrees of bank and do not exceed VNE, VLE or VFE [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

steps.s: Passing FL 200 the descent is established and stable. The learner wants to keep going at idle to 10,000 ft.
options: Continue to 10,000 ft at idle
End the practice descent now
Climb back up and repeat it twice
Shut down the engine to simulate a failure too
steps.why: In training, end the descent once established; prolonged practice overcools piston cylinders [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].

steps.s: On the ground after the flight. How do you open the debrief?
options: Hand over a list of errors
Ask the learner to assess the flight first, then compare it with yours
Sign the endorsement and skip the debrief
Tell them it was perfect
steps.why: Collaborative assessment starts with learner self-assessment; give concrete suggestions and avoid ending negatively [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].
